question_en: An investor buys a newly issued 20-year bond at par. The bond pays a 6% annual coupon. Shortly after purchase, the bond's YTM falls to 5% and stays at that level until the bond is sold at the end of three years. If the reinvestment rate over the period is 5%, the investor's annualized rate of return over the three-year investment horizon is closest to:
explanation_en:
The rate of return (or horizon return) is the geometric average annual rate that equates the initial investment with the value accumulated by
the end of the holding period (ie, investment horizon). The accumulated value, or total money return, is the sum of:
price at which the bond is sold
cumulative coupon payments
reinvestment income on any coupons received before the end of the holding period
These three components can be computed in two steps. The bond must be priced at a 5% yield three years in the future (when 17 years remain
until maturity). The coupon payments plus reinvestment income are calculated simultaneously by solving for the future value of an annuity.
The total money return divided by the initial investment is equal to 1 + the total rate of return. That outcome is annualized by raising it to the power
of (1/holding period) and subtracting 1 (ie, removing the value of the initial investment).
(Choice A) 8.94% uses a total money return reflecting only the bond price and the three coupons received over the investment horizon. This
solution omits the reinvestment income on the first two coupons.
(Choice C) 10.06% is the arithmetic (rather than the standard geometric) average annual return. 10.06% is based on the accurate total rate of
return (30.19%) divided by 3, rather than (1 + total rate of return)1/3 – 1.

subtopic: 7.09 The Term Structure of Interest Rates Spot, Par, and Forward Curves
question_en:
An investor with a 5-year investment horizon observes the following annual compound spot rates:

| Tenor | Spot Rate |
|---|---|
| 1-year | 2.50% |
| 2-year | 2.90% |
| 3-year | 3.20% |
| 4-year | 3.40% |
| 5-year | 3.50% |

Given the observed spot rates, the 3y2y implied forward rate is closest to:
explanation_en: Implied forward rates (IFRs), also known as forward yields, are future period interest rates that reflect the difference between spot rates of different tenors (ie, maturities). Spot rates are the YTMs on zero-coupon bonds. The IFR for the period between two spot rates of different maturities is a reinvestment rate that results in two strategies, each having an investment horizon equal to the longer-maturity spot rate, earning the same rate of return. In this question, given the stipulated investment horizon and spot rates, the two strategies are: Invest at the 3-year spot rate and then, at the end of 3 years, reinvest the maturity value at a rate equal to today's 3y2y IFR (ie, the 2-year rate starting 3 years in the future). Invest at the 5-year spot rate and hold for 5 years. Since IFRs are reinvestment rates that result in two strategies earning equal rates of return, forward rates are referred to as breakeven reinvestment rates. The 3y2y IFR (ie, the 2-year forward rate starting 3 years in the future, or IFR ) is calculated as 3.95%: 3,5 − 3 (Choice A) 3.55% is the 1y2y IFR (ie, 2-year forward rate starting 1 year in the future). (Choice B) 3.90% is the 2y3y IFR (ie, 3-year forward rate starting 2 years in the future).

subtopic: Reading 66 Asset-Backed Security (ABS) Instrument and Market Features
question_en: A covered bond that may postpone the originally scheduled maturity date by as much as a year to delay default is:
explanation_en: A soft-bullet covered bond may postpone the originally scheduled maturity date by as much as a year to delay default. A hard-bullet covered bond is in default if the issuer fails to make a scheduled payment. A conditional pass-through covered bond converts to a pass-through bond on the maturity date if any payments remain due.

question_en: The bootstrap method of estimating the standard error of sample means involves drawing repeated samples from a data set, each with:
explanation_en: The bootstrap method involves drawing repeated samples of size n from the same data set and calculating the standard deviation of the resulting sample means. The jackknife method involves calculating multiple means from the same sample, each with one observation removed, and calculating the standard deviation of those means.

subtopic: 3.01 Portfolio Risk And Return Part I
question_en: In determining the optimal portfolio for an investor, which of the following factors is best determined for each investor?
explanation_en:
Each investor's risk aversion determines the investor's utility and helps that investor choose the optimal investor portfolio. An indifference
curve represents the set of all portfolio combinations of return and risk with the same utility. Since all portfolios on the same curve provide the
same utility, each investor is indifferent in selecting any portfolio on it.
An optimal investor portfolio is represented by the point of tangency between the indifference curve and the capital allocation line. The
capital allocation line represents portfolios that dominate all other portfolios with respect to risk and return. It is a straight line that originates from
the risk-free rate and touches the efficient frontier.
(Choice B) All investors have the same risk-free rate of lending. That rate does not impact how an investor chooses the optimal portfolio on the
capital allocation line.
(Choice C) Each viable portfolio has an expected return and portfolio standard deviation (portfolio risk). Plotting these portfolios by risk and
expected return represents the investment opportunity set. All investors have the same investment opportunity set.

question_en: Direct investment in infrastructure is most similar to investing in:
explanation_en: Investing in infrastructure is most similar to investing in commercial real estate because both involve real, illiquid, capital intensive, long-term assets that require large investment amounts and specialized knowledge. Both publicly traded stocks and government debt investments are easily accessible with lower minimum investments, do not require additional capital investment, and are highly liquid.

explanation_en:
Financial ratios can be useful indicators of a company's health and performance and therefore are used extensively in financial analysis. Ratios
typically require context, either comparing them to other companies or to the same ratio in prior periods.
In this scenario, the level of debt affects all three ratios. The debt-to-equity ratio and financial leverage ratio both measure a company's leverage.
Greater proportions of debt increase a company's leverage, causing both ratios to increase. Debt also increases a company's interest expense,

ROE is a profitability ratio that measures the return (ie, net income) earned by a company's equity shareholders. Higher ROE ratios indicate a
higher rate of return for each dollar of equity invested. In this scenario, equity must be calculated before calculating ROE. Liabilities are used to

subtopic: 7.12 Yield-Based Bond Convexity and Portfolio Properties
question_en: If a noncallable bond has an annual modified duration of 9.718 and an annual convexity of 167.574, the estimated percentage price increase if its YTM declines by 50 basis points is closest to:
explanation_en:
Duration and convexity can be used to estimate percentage changes in bond prices. Modified duration measures the change in a bond's price for
a given change in its YTM, and convexity measures the change in the bond's price sensitivity.
Duration-based estimates of price change reflect the inverse relationship between bond prices and yields. To capture the direction of price
sensitivity changes, the price impact of convexity should be:
added to the percentage price change due to duration when YTM declines and
subtracted from the percentage price change due to duration when YTM increases.
(Choice A) 4.65% results from mistakenly subtracting the convexity impact of the price change estimated from the bond's modified duration rather
than adding it. Convexity reduces bond price declines when interest rates rise, but increases price appreciation when a bond's YTM decreases.
(Choice B) 4.86% is the estimated price change due to the bond's modified duration, but it fails to account for the bond's convexity.

question_en: For an investor with a long-term investment horizon, the most appropriate response to a new, high-velocity geopolitical risk is to adjust a portfolio's:
explanation_en: Framework for assessing geopolitical risks Likelihood Probability that a geopolitical risk will occur Velocity How quickly the risk will impact investment returns Impact Size of impact and breadth of impact Analysts evaluate geopolitical risks by assessing the: likelihood that they will occur, velocity of impact, and size and nature of impact. Velocity describes the speed of impact on investment returns. High-velocity risks have short-term impacts and create short-term market volatility (eg, 1987 stock market crash). Investors may capitalize on such market dislocations via tactical asset allocations (ie, short-term shifts in asset class composition of a portfolio). (Choice A) Investors typically shift sector allocations in response to medium-velocity risks, which have medium-term impacts and may negatively impact a company's operations and reduce cash flows, thereby reducing valuation (eg, a crop disease decimates potato harvests for more than one season). (Choice C) Changes to strategic asset allocation may be warranted by low-velocity risks that have major long-term impacts due to changes to asset class returns and risks.

subtopic: Reading 18 Capital Flows and the FX Market
question_en: A country's central bank announces a monetary policy goal of a stable exchange rate with the euro, which it defines as deviations of no more than 3% from its current exchange rate of 2.5000. The country's exchange rate regime is best described as a:
explanation_en: This exchange rate regime is best described as a target zone, or a system of pegged exchange rates within horizontal bands. A target zone allows wider exchange rate fluctuations than a conventional fixed peg arrangement, which typically limits the permitted range to within 1% of the pegged exchange rate. Management of exchange rates within crawling bands allows the percentage deviation from the pegged exchange rate to increase over time.

question_en: An investor who wants to add equity securities to her portfolio that will be relatively uncorrelated with changes in business cycles should most likely look for companies that produce:
explanation_en: Nondurable goods are goods which only have value for relatively short periods of time (such as food and gasoline). They are needed regardless of what happens in the economy, so their usage will be relatively uncorrelated to changes in business cycles. Durable goods tend to be higher value, longer lasting items with cyclical demand. Some services (e.g, travel) are discretionary and therefore cyclical while others (e.g., health care) are less so.

subtopic: Reading 50 Fixed-Income Cash Flows and Types
question_en: Which of the following statements with regard to floating rate notes that have caps and floors is most accurate? A oor is a disadvantage to both the issuer and the bondholder while a cap is an
option_a: advantage to both the issuer and the bondholder. A cap is a disadvantage to the bondholder while a oor is a disadvantage to the
option_b: issuer. A cap is an advantage to the bondholder while a oor is an advantage to the
explanation_en: A cap limits the upside potential of the coupon rate paid on the floating rate bond and is therefore a disadvantage to the bondholder. A floor limits the downside potential of the coupon rate and is therefore a disadvantage to the bond issuer.

question_en: An investor buys a bond for 115.443470 per 100 par value. The bond has 10 years left until maturity, a 5% YTM, and a 7% annual coupon. Four years later, the bond is sold for 112.894681 at a YTM of 4.5%. The capital gain or loss is closest to a:
explanation_en:
The capital gain or loss on a bond trade is the difference between the selling price and the bond's carrying value, not the purchase price.
For bonds sold prior to maturity, the carrying value is the present value of the remaining cash flows, using the YTM at purchase, not the current
YTM, to discount those remaining cash flows.
Since they must converge with par value by maturity, the carrying values for bonds purchased at a premium decline over time. Although the bond
in this instance sold for less than its purchase price, its sale price was higher than its carrying value, so there is a capital gain.
(Choice A) A 2.5488 loss is the result of using the original purchase price rather than the carrying value.
(Choice C) A 3.6286 gain results from using straight-line amortization of the purchase premium to determine the carrying value.

Sector indexes are used to track the investment performance of a given sector and may include stocks from a single industry (eg,

subtopic: 7.13 Curve-Based and Empirical Fixed-Income Risk Measures
question_en: An investor is evaluating several callable bonds. The investor believes short-term interest rates are likely to rise significantly, but intermediate and long-term rates will be stable. Which of the following types of duration would be most appropriate for evaluating the risk of the bonds given the expected flattening of the yield curve?
explanation_en: Effective duration estimates how much a bond's total price will change in response to a parallel shift of the benchmark yield curve. Since effective duration uses the yield curve instead of the YTM, it is a more appropriate measure of interest rate risk for bonds that have embedded options, such as callable and putable bonds. Those bonds have unpredictable cash flows due to the possibility of option exercise and thus lack a well-defined YTM. (Choices B and C) For bonds that have predictable cash flows, and thus a well-defined YTM, interest rate risk can be measured using approximate modified duration, which is based on YTM.

question_en: An analyst relies on summary forecasting measures including earnings per share and free cash flow metrics in estimating a company's future financial data. Which of the following features is an advantage of using this forecasting approach?
explanation_en: Relying on summary measures is useful when the data is stable and predictable or if issuer disclosures are limited. This approach is efficient in the sense that the analyst relies on relatively few variables. Disadvantages of this approach are less transparency and greater difficulty in auditing the forecasts.

question_en: An analyst compiles the following data about an equity-indexed annuity that pays one of five possible returns to investors each year: The expected value of the asset's return is closest to:
explanation_en:
The expected value of a random variable is the probability-weighted average of the variable's possible outcomes. The term "expected value"
is used with a random variable, whose value is not yet determined. In calculating the expected value, each outcome is weighted by the likelihood
of its occurrence.
In this scenario, multiply each return by its probability, and then sum the resulting products to calculate the expected value:
The historical occurrences of the last 10 years are not used in the calculation of the expected value.
(Choice B) 3.00% is the simple arithmetic average of the five returns, not accounting for their number of occurrences.
(Choice C) 3.10% is the average of the values of the samples observed, in this case: [(1 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 5) / 10] = 3.10. The
expected value should not be confused with the sample mean, which is used with historical data.

question_en: Which of the following types of derivatives most likely gives the buyer a right but no obligation to trade the underlying?
explanation_en: Derivative contract comparison Forward commitments Contingent claims Contract Exchange of obligations Conveyance of rights Buyer has the right, but no obligation, to exercise; seller's Counterparties Both obligated to perform obligation is contingent on exercise Cost at Usually no cost to either party Buyer pays premium to seller initiation Examples Futures, forwards, most swaps Options, credit default swaps, total return swaps Derivative contracts are designated as either forward commitment contracts or contingent claims. Contingent claims are conveyances of rights in which buyers can choose whether to go through with the transaction (ie, exercise their right) and in which sellers are obligated only to perform if buyers exercise. Examples of contingent claims include the following: Options: Buyers acquire the right to buy (ie, call options) or sell (ie, put options) an underlying asset at a specified price at a future date, but the right does not have to be exercised. Sellers are obligated to sell (buy) only if the option is exercised. Credit default swaps (CDS): CDS are equivalent to credit options. If the underlying bond defaults, the CDS buyer can exercise its right to force the CDS seller to buy the defaulted bond. Forward commitment contracts are exchanges of contractual obligations in which buyers and sellers commit to a future transaction. Examples of forward commitment contracts include the following: Forward or futures contracts: Counterparties commit to exchange an asset for a specified price at a specified time in the future. A bond futures contract is a forward commitment (Choice A). Fixed-for-floating interest rate swaps: Counterparties commit to exchange a stream of fixed interest payments from the fixed-rate payer for a stream of floating interest payments from the fixed-rate receiver (Choice B).

subtopic: Reading 80 Investments in Private Capital- Equity and Debt
question_en: Which of the following types of private debt has the lowest level of risk?
explanation_en: Unitranche debt is a blend of different classes of debt and typically ranks between senior and subordinated debt. Mezzanine debt is subordinated to senior debt and often unsecured. Venture debt is the riskiest because it finances start-up companies that have high business risk and often lack positive cash flow and assets.

option_a: the goal is to test the sensitivity of assumptions. the change in the credit spread is positively correlated with the change in the
option_b: benchmark yield curve. the change in the credit spread is negatively correlated with the change in the

subtopic: 7.12 Yield-Based Bond Convexity and Portfolio Properties
question_en: A noncallable bond has a 6% YTM based on annual compounding. The bond has an annual modified duration of 18.868 and an annual convexity of 372.027. If the bond's yield is expected to increase to 6.20%, the expected price change is closest to:
explanation_en:
The price impact of a change in a bond's YTM can be estimated using duration and convexity. Estimates based on duration capture most of
the price change but fail to reflect the change in price sensitivity as yield changes. Adjusting for a bond's convexity greatly improves the accuracy
of price change estimates.
The impact of convexity is always positive for noncallable bonds. As yields fall, prices become more sensitive to yield changes (ie, bonds
appreciate more rapidly). As yields rise, prices become less sensitive to yield changes (ie, prices decline more slowly). The convexity impact is
added to duration-based estimates of price change when prices are rising; price declines are reduced by the convexity impact.
(Choice A) −3.85% results from summing the convexity impact with the percentage price decline based on duration.
(Choice C) −3.33% results from failing to square the yield change and then not properly adjusting the decimal point when calculating the
convexity impact.

question_en: Yield spreads tend to widen when equity market performance is:
explanation_en: Conditions that cause equity markets to weaken, such as poor economic growth, also tend to widen yield spreads in the bond market. Likewise, strong equity market performance tends to coincide with narrowing yield spreads. Yield spreads tend to narrow when equity markets are stable because investors "reaching for yield" increase their demand for bonds.

subtopic: Reading 86 Basics of Portfolio Planning and Construction
question_en: Which of the following would least likely be considered a minimum requirement of an IPS? A(n):
option_b: investment strategy based on client circumstances and constraints.
explanation_en: An IPS does not necessarily, or even typically, require a target return because future market movements are either difficult or impossible to predict with any degree of accuracy. At a minimum the IPS should contain a clear statement of client circumstances and constraints, and investment strategy consistent with these, and a benchmark portfolio or instrument against which to evaluate portfolio returns.
